subject: AP Human Geography
source_note: Structured from the AP Human Geography Course and Exam Description (© 2020). Unit titles follow the CED's framework. Essential questions are written for this app; skill descriptions are paraphrased, not quoted.

units.title: Unit 1: Thinking Geographically
essential_questions: Every map is a set of choices about what to leave out. Take one you have used this week and say what its omissions cost.
Is geography better understood as the study of place, or of the relationships between places? Argue one.
When does zooming out to a global scale reveal something, and when does it hide the thing that matters?
focus_skills: Say precisely what the concept means and use it correctly in a real case
Read the map, chart or table for what it actually shows before you interpret it
Ask what changes when you zoom in or out — what appears, and what disappears
texts: Bring the map, chart or article you are working from — we will read it together rather than talk around it

units.title: Unit 2: Population and Migration
essential_questions: Two countries can share a fertility rate and face completely different futures. What else has to be true for that?
Malthus has been wrong for two centuries. Is the model useless, or is it waiting?
Push and pull factors are taught as a tidy pair. Take a real migration and say which framing distorts it.
focus_skills: Say precisely what the concept means and use it correctly in a real case
Describe a spatial pattern, then explain what produces it and what it produces
Read the map, chart or table for what it actually shows before you interpret it

units.title: Unit 3: Cultural Patterns and Processes
essential_questions: A cultural landscape is a record of who had power. Read one you know and say what it records.
Does globalisation homogenise culture or intensify local identity? Find a case that resists your answer.
Language and religion diffuse differently. What accounts for the difference?

units.title: Unit 4: Political Patterns and Processes
essential_questions: A boundary drawn by outsiders and one drawn by locals can look identical on a map. What makes them behave differently?
Is the nation-state still the basic unit of political geography, or a category we have not updated?
Devolution and supranationalism pull in opposite directions. Can a state experience both at once? Show it.

units.title: Unit 5: Agriculture and Rural Land Use
essential_questions: Von Thünen's model assumes a flat, uniform plain. What does it still explain despite that, and what does it get wrong?
The Green Revolution raised yields and concentrated ownership. On balance, was it a success?
Who actually decides what a farmer plants? Trace the chain and say where the real power sits.

units.title: Unit 6: Cities and Urban Land Use
essential_questions: The concentric zone, sector and multiple nuclei models were built from a handful of cities. Test one against a city you know.
Gentrification improves buildings and displaces people. How would you decide whether a neighbourhood is better off?
What makes a city sustainable — its density, its transport, its politics? Rank them.

units.title: Unit 7: Industrial and Economic Development
essential_questions: GDP per capita and the Human Development Index can rank two countries in opposite orders. Which would you trust, and for what question?
Rostow says development is a sequence. Wallerstein says it is a structure. Which better explains a country you have studied?
Is sustainable development a real goal or a phrase that lets everyone agree? Defend your answer.
